title: Chlorine radical-mediated electrochemical propylene epoxidation from seawater

paper_content.abstract:
Electrocatalytic chlorine-mediated propylene oxidation utilizing seawater represents a
promising route for sustainable propylene oxide (PO) synthesis. Unfortunately, inefficient
utilization of active chlorine species results in compromised yield and Faradaic efficiency (F.E.).
Herein, we achieve efficient chlorine radical-mediated propylene to PO by incorporating Li into
Co O , attaining a PO F.E. approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m2/h in simulated seawater
3 4
with long-term stability for over 100 h. Furthermore, a PO yield of 78.9 mol/m2/h is obtained even
under an industrial-level current density of 0.5 A cm-2, demonstrating competitive performance
compared with most reported noble metal catalysts. Mechanistic investigations reveal that Li
doping transforms the adsorption configuration of Cl– on Co O from linear Co-Cl structure to
3 4
more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation, and
consequently redirecting propylene oxidation from conventional HClO pathway to a more efficient
•Cl route. This work advances the mechanistic understanding of the mechanism of electrocatalytic
propylene oxidation and offers great opportunities for the sustainable synthesis of commercial
chemicals using waste lithium-ion batteries, seawater, and renewable electricity.
paper_content.introduction:
Propylene oxide (PO) is a crucial industrial intermediate, serving as a precursor to a variety of
commercial chemicals including polymers, propylene glycol, polyurethane foams, and propylene
carbonate.1 It ranks as the third most significant propylene derivative with an annual global
production exceeding 10 million tonnes.2 Conventional industrial methods for PO production
include chlorohydrin process, hydrogen peroxide-based process (HPPO) and Halcon process (Fig.
1a-c).3 Nevertheless, these methods face challenges such as high costs, generation of
stoichiometric side products and severe pollution.4 Therefore, there is an urgent demand to develop
a more sustainable PO synthetic route. The electrochemical oxidation of propylene driven by
renewable electricity presents a promising alternative for PO production under ambient
conditions.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 While direct electrooxidation via water-derived active oxygen species offers
a viable route but is severely hindered by propylene’s poor solubility and inevitable overoxidation,
resulting in limited Faradaic efficiency (F.E.) (<70%), low current density (<10 mA cm-2) and
insufficient stability (<12 h), rendering the efficiency of direct electrocatalytic oxidation of
propylene far from satisfactory (Fig. 1d).11, 12, 13, 14

The indirect chlorination-mediated route overcomes these limitations by integrating
electrochemical chloroxidation with propylene oxidation, enabling stable chloropropanol
production which subsequently reacts with the base generated from the cathodic hydrogen
evolution reaction to yield PO (Fig. 1e).2 Notably, besides serving as a redox mediator, chloride
provide the additional advantage of allowing direct use of seawater as the electrolyte. Current
studies identify hypochlorous acid (HClO) as the active species in chlorination-mediated olefin
oxidation, generated through the oxidation of Cl– to Cl

with high efficiency remains a significant challenge.

Chlorine radicals (•Cl), as a potent oxidant with high oxidation potentials (2.47 V) have been an
appealing option for mediating various oxidation reactions.20, 21, 22, 23, 24 As an electrophilic reagent,
•Cl can react with unsaturated organics such as olefins in addition reactions to form C-Cl bonds
by generating a stabilized secondary carbon-centered radical.25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30 Therefore, the
utilization of •Cl holds great promise for achieving efficient propylene oxidation. During
electrochemical chloroxidation, •Cl is typically produced via the Volmer step.31 Nevertheless, the
marked tendency of •Cl to mutual couple to generate Cl limits its effective utilization. Modulating
2

coupling. For instance, Zhang et al. utilized discontinuous Cl– adsorption sites to inhibit Cl
2

et al. enhanced •Cl utilization by increasing the spatial separation between •Cl species, which
mitigated mutual recombination and facilitated the •Cl-mediated epoxide ring-opening process.33
However, due to the lack of direct regulation over the intrinsic adsorption behavior of Cl–, the
utilization efficiency of •Cl remains suboptimal.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Ming Cheng and co-workers report electrochemical propylene oxide synthesis using Li–Co3O4 catalysts. The authors claim that Li doping reconfigures chloride adsorption on the cobalt oxide surface, thereby promoting a chlorine radical–mediated pathway. They support this with spectroscopic analyses (EPR, FT-IR) and computational studies. The catalytic performance is impressive, and the mechanistic proposal is intriguing. I would recommend publication after the following issues are addressed:
i) A central claim is that propylene oxidation proceeds via chlorine radicals. The in situ EPR study is presented as key evidence, but the Methods section lacks critical details. Please provide a clear description of the spin-trapping protocol (concentration of trapping agents, timing of addition, acquisition parameters). Also, control experiments should be conducted to confirm that spin traps do not interfere with the electrolysis.
ii) The EPR data suggest the involvement of both •Cl and •OH, yet only tert-butanol quenching is reported. Additional radical scavengers or spin trapping (e.g., benzoquinone, BMPO (5-tert-Butoxycarbonyl-5-methyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide), or TEMPO) would provide complementary mechanistic evidence.
iii) The manuscript emphasizes chlorine radicals but also shows stronger •OH signals. The authors attribute this to H2O activation at oxygen vacancies. How do •Cl and •OH interact in the reaction network? Is there any possibility of overoxidation by •OH at higher potentials that could compromise PO selectivity?
iv) A D2O/H2O kinetic isotope effect (KIE) study may help to confirm the hydroxyl involvement in the epoxidation process.
v) Electrochemical analysis requires clarification. Potentials are presented without iR-compensation and referenced to Ag/AgCl, making comparisons with CER/OER a bit ambiguous. Please provide iR-corrected polarization curves, convert potentials to the RHE scale, and quantify solution resistance and membrane contributions by EIS. Reported onset shifts and performance enhancements should be re-evaluated accordingly, to show that the obtained results are intrinsic to Li doping rather than ohmic artifacts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, the authors successfully incorporated Li into Co3O4 via flash Joule heating treatment, attained a remarkable propylene oxide (PO) Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a production rate of 20.6 mol m-2 h-1 in simulated neutral seawater, along with excellent stability exceeding 100 hours. Mechanistic investigations revealed that HClO was the primary active species in the Co3O4-catalyzed oxidation process, while on Li-Co3O4, the more efficient •Cl pathway becomes dominant. This shift in reaction mechanism is attributed to the Li doping transformed the Cl- adsorption configuration from a linear Co-Cl structure to a more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation. This work not only demonstrates a promising route for utilizing seawater resources in organic synthesis but also offers new mechanistic insights into chlorine-mediated electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. However, there are some shortcomings in the manuscripts.
1. In this paper, the author highlights the advantages of the •Cl pathway over the HClO route. However, radicals are generally known for their inherent lack of selectivity. Why the •Cl-mediated process in this system still achieves high selectivity towards propylene oxide? The author should give more discussion.
2. In Figure 3b, the RuIrTi electrode shows the highest HClO production, yet the Faradaic efficiency for PO is comparable to that of Co3O4. This observation appears inconsistent and needs further explanation.
3. In Figure 4c, the experimental Raman spectrum lacks the peak at 155 cm-1 that is present in the simulated spectrum. The author should give more discussion.
4. In line 275, the formation of HClO on Co3O4 is attributed to the evolution of Cl2. However, HClO could also be generated through the direct oxidation of Cl- (Appl. Catal. B-Environ. Energy 2025, 361, 124644). The authors should provide the corresponding evidence.
5. In the proposed mechanism, the authors suggest that transient and highly reactive •OH attacks transient carbon radical intermediates to form chloropropanol. However, the selectivity and efficiency of coupling between two transient, highly reactive free radicals are theoretically limited (Sci. China Chem. 2025, 68, 3770-3777, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2018, 140, 2438−2441). The authors should reconsider this pathway or supply additional data to validate the role of •OH.
6. Figure 3a shows a significant enhancement in the Cl⁻ reduction peak intensity following the addition and removal of cyclopropane, despite no theoretical change in chloride ion concentration. The authors should provide an explanation and discussion for this discrepancy.
7. All electrode potentials presented in the text and figures should be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale to ensure consistent and standardized reporting.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the author designed a catalyst by doping lithium recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries into Co₃O₄, enabling highly efficient electrocatalytic synthesis of propylene oxide in simulated seawater via enhanced active chlorine generation. This whole work not only offers new insights into the mechanism of propylene epoxidation but also opens a new pathway for environmentally sustainable and low-cost synthesis of industrial chemicals. There are only two minor questions that need to be supplemented:
1. The Li-Co₃O₄ catalyst exhibited good stability during the 100-hour test. Is there any data indicating that Li⁺ does not leach or migrate under strong anodic polarization conditions? Is it necessary to perform post-reaction characterization (such as ICP or XPS) of the catalyst to confirm the retention of Li and the local structural stability?
2. In the catalyst preparation process, flash Joule heating was employed to treat Li-doped Co₃O₄. The article merely mentioned the treatment steps without elaborating on the relevant flash Joule heating parameters (such as heating rate, holding time). The author may supplement as necessary.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This study presents a incorporates lithium into Co₃O₄ via flash Joule heating treatment, achieving efficient chlorine radical-mediated conversion of propylene to propylene oxide (PO), with an excellent PO Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m²/h in simulated neutral seawater, maintaining long-term stability for over 100 hours. This study provides new insights into the mechanism of electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. Overall, this work holds potential for publication in Nature Communications, but several major issues must be addressed to enhance experimental rigor and clarity before I can recommend for its publication.
Major revisions:
1. Through FT-EXAFS analysis, the authors concluded that Li preferentially replaces tetrahedral Co sites (as evidenced by the significant weakening of the Co-Co Td signal) and constructed a corresponding structural model. Did the authors perform theoretical calculations to support this selective replacement tendency? What is the energy difference between Li⁺ entering tetrahedral and octahedral sites? Are there other possible Li occupation sites (such as interstitial sites)?
2. The TOF-SIMS results (Figures 1c-1d) showed a higher concentration of Li in fractured flake regions. Does this imply that the Li doping process is influenced by material morphology or defect density? Could such non-uniform distribution induce compromise the reproducibility of overall catalytic performance?
3. Multiple characterization techniques indicated that Li has entered the lattice and induced changes in electronic structure and local coordination environment, however, no noticeable peak shifts were observed in the XRD patterns (Figure S2). Could the authors explain why no detectable lattice expansion or contraction occurs upon Li doping? Is this due to the low doping level, or could it be attributed to the similar ionic radii of Li⁺ and Co²⁺? Please provide ICP or other quantitative analyses to confirm the actual Li doping content.
4. In the active chlorine (AC) generation (Figure S11) and propylene oxidation tests (Figure 2b), for both Co₃O₄ and RuIrTi catalysts, the lost Faradaic efficiency, could this be attributed to OER or other side reactions? At least, the FE for OER should be measured at one potential to clarify the fate of the missing electrons (FE).
5. During the stability test in Figure 2h, the reaction potential is extremely high (up to 3.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl or may be > 4 V vs. RHE?), which appears inconsistent with the LSV results in Figure 2a. This observation is quite surprising, as both the catalysts and carbon paper substrate remain stable at such a high potential. Have the authors did any characterizations of the catalyst after stability reaction?
6. Theoretical calculations suggest that the OER energy barrier is reduced on Li-Co₃O₄ (Figure 3i). However, during the OER test in Figure 2a, the OER performance of Li-Co₃O₄ shows no improvement compared to Co₃O₄, which seems contradictory. Could the authors discuss this discrepancy?
7. The authors employ several characterization techniques commonly used in thermal catalysis studies (such as H₂ temperature-programmed reduction (H₂-TPR) in Figure 4d and temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) in Figure 4e) to investigate species adsorption. However, the real electrochemical environment involves a solid–liquid interface. So can these gas-phase-based methods or characterizations accurately reflect the adsorption behavior of the catalyst under actual operating conditions?
8. Why is the formation of Cl* on Li-Co₃O₄ thermodynamically spontaneous (Figure 5g)? Were the theoretical calculations performed under applied electrode potential?
Other minor comments:
1. Regarding the O 1s XPS spectra, more detailed assignment of different oxygen species should be provided, rather than simply labeling them with α, β or γ.
2. The manuscript should include more experimental details. The current version lacks sufficient information, making it confusing and difficult to follow. For example, various reaction solutions, including artificial seawater and real seawater are used in experiments in Figure 2. The exact composition of the artificial seawater should be specified, and it should be clarified whether the electrolytes used in Figure 2g–2h are identical to those in Figure 2a.
3. The LSV tests with propylene and NaCl should also be provided, similar to Figure 2a.
4. The assignment of EPR signals for Cl• and OH• radicals should be supported by cited references or spectral simulations in Figure 3d.

## Abstract

Electrocatalytic chlorine-mediated propylene oxidation utilizing seawater represents a
promising route for sustainable propylene oxide (PO) synthesis. Unfortunately, inefficient
utilization of active chlorine species results in compromised yield and Faradaic efficiency (F.E.).
Herein, we achieve efficient chlorine radical-mediated propylene to PO by incorporating Li into
Co O , attaining a PO F.E. approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m2/h in simulated seawater
3 4
with long-term stability for over 100 h. Furthermore, a PO yield of 78.9 mol/m2/h is obtained even
under an industrial-level current density of 0.5 A cm-2, demonstrating competitive performance
compared with most reported noble metal catalysts. Mechanistic investigations reveal that Li
doping transforms the adsorption configuration of Cl– on Co O from linear Co-Cl structure to
3 4
more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation, and
consequently redirecting propylene oxidation from conventional HClO pathway to a more efficient
•Cl route. This work advances the mechanistic understanding of the mechanism of electrocatalytic
propylene oxidation and offers great opportunities for the sustainable synthesis of commercial
chemicals using waste lithium-ion batteries, seawater, and renewable electricity.

## Introduction

Propylene oxide (PO) is a crucial industrial intermediate, serving as a precursor to a variety of
commercial chemicals including polymers, propylene glycol, polyurethane foams, and propylene
carbonate.1 It ranks as the third most significant propylene derivative with an annual global
production exceeding 10 million tonnes.2 Conventional industrial methods for PO production
include chlorohydrin process, hydrogen peroxide-based process (HPPO) and Halcon process (Fig.
1a-c).3 Nevertheless, these methods face challenges such as high costs, generation of
stoichiometric side products and severe pollution.4 Therefore, there is an urgent demand to develop
a more sustainable PO synthetic route. The electrochemical oxidation of propylene driven by
renewable electricity presents a promising alternative for PO production under ambient
conditions.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 While direct electrooxidation via water-derived active oxygen species offers
a viable route but is severely hindered by propylene’s poor solubility and inevitable overoxidation,
resulting in limited Faradaic efficiency (F.E.) (<70%), low current density (<10 mA cm-2) and
insufficient stability (<12 h), rendering the efficiency of direct electrocatalytic oxidation of
propylene far from satisfactory (Fig. 1d).11, 12, 13, 14

The indirect chlorination-mediated route overcomes these limitations by integrating
electrochemical chloroxidation with propylene oxidation, enabling stable chloropropanol
production which subsequently reacts with the base generated from the cathodic hydrogen
evolution reaction to yield PO (Fig. 1e).2 Notably, besides serving as a redox mediator, chloride
provide the additional advantage of allowing direct use of seawater as the electrolyte. Current
studies identify hypochlorous acid (HClO) as the active species in chlorination-mediated olefin

Chlorine radicals (•Cl), as a potent oxidant with high oxidation potentials (2.47 V) have been an
appealing option for mediating various oxidation reactions.20, 21, 22, 23, 24 As an electrophilic reagent,
•Cl can react with unsaturated organics such as olefins in addition reactions to form C-Cl bonds
by generating a stabilized secondary carbon-centered radical.25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30 Therefore, the
utilization of •Cl holds great promise for achieving efficient propylene oxidation. During
electrochemical chloroxidation, •Cl is typically produced via the Volmer step.31 Nevertheless, the

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Ming Cheng and co-workers report electrochemical propylene oxide synthesis using Li–Co3O4 catalysts. The authors claim that Li doping reconfigures chloride adsorption on the cobalt oxide surface, thereby promoting a chlorine radical–mediated pathway. They support this with spectroscopic analyses (EPR, FT-IR) and computational studies. The catalytic performance is impressive, and the mechanistic proposal is intriguing. I would recommend publication after the following issues are addressed:
i) A central claim is that propylene oxidation proceeds via chlorine radicals. The in situ EPR study is presented as key evidence, but the Methods section lacks critical details. Please provide a clear description of the spin-trapping protocol (concentration of trapping agents, timing of addition, acquisition parameters). Also, control experiments should be conducted to confirm that spin traps do not interfere with the electrolysis.
ii) The EPR data suggest the involvement of both •Cl and •OH, yet only tert-butanol quenching is reported. Additional radical scavengers or spin trapping (e.g., benzoquinone, BMPO (5-tert-Butoxycarbonyl-5-methyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide), or TEMPO) would provide complementary mechanistic evidence.
iii) The manuscript emphasizes chlorine radicals but also shows stronger •OH signals. The authors attribute this to H2O activation at oxygen vacancies. How do •Cl and •OH interact in the reaction network? Is there any possibility of overoxidation by •OH at higher potentials that could compromise PO selectivity?
iv) A D2O/H2O kinetic isotope effect (KIE) study may help to confirm the hydroxyl involvement in the epoxidation process.
v) Electrochemical analysis requires clarification. Potentials are presented without iR-compensation and referenced to Ag/AgCl, making comparisons with CER/OER a bit ambiguous. Please provide iR-corrected polarization curves, convert potentials to the RHE scale, and quantify solution resistance and membrane contributions by EIS. Reported onset shifts and performance enhancements should be re-evaluated accordingly, to show that the obtained results are intrinsic to Li doping rather than ohmic artifacts.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors successfully incorporated Li into Co3O4 via flash Joule heating treatment, attained a remarkable propylene oxide (PO) Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a production rate of 20.6 mol m-2 h-1 in simulated neutral seawater, along with excellent stability exceeding 100 hours. Mechanistic investigations revealed that HClO was the primary active species in the Co3O4-catalyzed oxidation process, while on Li-Co3O4, the more efficient •Cl pathway becomes dominant. This shift in reaction mechanism is attributed to the Li doping transformed the Cl- adsorption configuration from a linear Co-Cl structure to a more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation. This work not only demonstrates a promising route for utilizing seawater resources in organic synthesis but also offers new mechanistic insights into chlorine-mediated electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. However, there are some shortcomings in the manuscripts.
1. In this paper, the author highlights the advantages of the •Cl pathway over the HClO route. However, radicals are generally known for their inherent lack of selectivity. Why the •Cl-mediated process in this system still achieves high selectivity towards propylene oxide? The author should give more discussion.
2. In Figure 3b, the RuIrTi electrode shows the highest HClO production, yet the Faradaic efficiency for PO is comparable to that of Co3O4. This observation appears inconsistent and needs further explanation.
3. In Figure 4c, the experimental Raman spectrum lacks the peak at 155 cm-1 that is present in the simulated spectrum. The author should give more discussion.
4. In line 275, the formation of HClO on Co3O4 is attributed to the evolution of Cl2. However, HClO could also be generated through the direct oxidation of Cl- (Appl. Catal. B-Environ. Energy 2025, 361, 124644). The authors should provide the corresponding evidence.
5. In the proposed mechanism, the authors suggest that transient and highly reactive •OH attacks transient carbon radical intermediates to form chloropropanol. However, the selectivity and efficiency of coupling between two transient, highly reactive free radicals are theoretically limited (Sci. China Chem. 2025, 68, 3770-3777, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2018, 140, 2438−2441). The authors should reconsider this pathway or supply additional data to validate the role of •OH.
6. Figure 3a shows a significant enhancement in the Cl⁻ reduction peak intensity following the addition and removal of cyclopropane, despite no theoretical change in chloride ion concentration. The authors should provide an explanation and discussion for this discrepancy.
7. All electrode potentials presented in the text and figures should be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale to ensure consistent and standardized reporting.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the author designed a catalyst by doping lithium recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries into Co₃O₄, enabling highly efficient electrocatalytic synthesis of propylene oxide in simulated seawater via enhanced active chlorine generation. This whole work not only offers new insights into the mechanism of propylene epoxidation but also opens a new pathway for environmentally sustainable and low-cost synthesis of industrial chemicals. There are only two minor questions that need to be supplemented:
1. The Li-Co₃O₄ catalyst exhibited good stability during the 100-hour test. Is there any data indicating that Li⁺ does not leach or migrate under strong anodic polarization conditions? Is it necessary to perform post-reaction characterization (such as ICP or XPS) of the catalyst to confirm the retention of Li and the local structural stability?
2. In the catalyst preparation process, flash Joule heating was employed to treat Li-doped Co₃O₄. The article merely mentioned the treatment steps without elaborating on the relevant flash Joule heating parameters (such as heating rate, holding time). The author may supplement as necessary.

### Reviewer 4

This study presents a incorporates lithium into Co₃O₄ via flash Joule heating treatment, achieving efficient chlorine radical-mediated conversion of propylene to propylene oxide (PO), with an excellent PO Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m²/h in simulated neutral seawater, maintaining long-term stability for over 100 hours. This study provides new insights into the mechanism of electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. Overall, this work holds potential for publication in Nature Communications, but several major issues must be addressed to enhance experimental rigor and clarity before I can recommend for its publication.
Major revisions:
1. Through FT-EXAFS analysis, the authors concluded that Li preferentially replaces tetrahedral Co sites (as evidenced by the significant weakening of the Co-Co Td signal) and constructed a corresponding structural model. Did the authors perform theoretical calculations to support this selective replacement tendency? What is the energy difference between Li⁺ entering tetrahedral and octahedral sites? Are there other possible Li occupation sites (such as interstitial sites)?
2. The TOF-SIMS results (Figures 1c-1d) showed a higher concentration of Li in fractured flake regions. Does this imply that the Li doping process is influenced by material morphology or defect density? Could such non-uniform distribution induce compromise the reproducibility of overall catalytic performance?
3. Multiple characterization techniques indicated that Li has entered the lattice and induced changes in electronic structure and local coordination environment, however, no noticeable peak shifts were observed in the XRD patterns (Figure S2). Could the authors explain why no detectable lattice expansion or contraction occurs upon Li doping? Is this due to the low doping level, or could it be attributed to the similar ionic radii of Li⁺ and Co²⁺? Please provide ICP or other quantitative analyses to confirm the actual Li doping content.
4. In the active chlorine (AC) generation (Figure S11) and propylene oxidation tests (Figure 2b), for both Co₃O₄ and RuIrTi catalysts, the lost Faradaic efficiency, could this be attributed to OER or other side reactions? At least, the FE for OER should be measured at one potential to clarify the fate of the missing electrons (FE).
5. During the stability test in Figure 2h, the reaction potential is extremely high (up to 3.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl or may be > 4 V vs. RHE?), which appears inconsistent with the LSV results in Figure 2a. This observation is quite surprising, as both the catalysts and carbon paper substrate remain stable at such a high potential. Have the authors did any characterizations of the catalyst after stability reaction?

So can these gas-phase-based methods or characterizations accurately reflect the adsorption behavior of the catalyst under actual operating conditions?
8. Why is the formation of Cl* on Li-Co₃O₄ thermodynamically spontaneous (Figure 5g)? Were the theoretical calculations performed under applied electrode potential?
Other minor comments:
1. Regarding the O 1s XPS spectra, more detailed assignment of different oxygen species should be provided, rather than simply labeling them with α, β or γ.
2. The manuscript should include more experimental details. The current version lacks sufficient information, making it confusing and difficult to follow. For example, various reaction solutions, including artificial seawater and real seawater are used in experiments in Figure 2. The exact composition of the artificial seawater should be specified, and it should be clarified whether the electrolytes used in Figure 2g–2h are identical to those in Figure 2a.
3. The LSV tests with propylene and NaCl should also be provided, similar to Figure 2a.
4. The assignment of EPR signals for Cl• and OH• radicals should be supported by cited references or spectral simulations in Figure 3d.

## Abstract

Electrocatalytic chlorine-mediated propylene oxidation utilizing seawater represents a
promising route for sustainable propylene oxide (PO) synthesis. Unfortunately, inefficient
utilization of active chlorine species results in compromised yield and Faradaic efficiency (F.E.).
Herein, we achieve efficient chlorine radical-mediated propylene to PO by incorporating Li into
Co O , attaining a PO F.E. approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m2/h in simulated seawater
3 4
with long-term stability for over 100 h. Furthermore, a PO yield of 78.9 mol/m2/h is obtained even
under an industrial-level current density of 0.5 A cm-2, demonstrating competitive performance
compared with most reported noble metal catalysts. Mechanistic investigations reveal that Li
doping transforms the adsorption configuration of Cl– on Co O from linear Co-Cl structure to
3 4
more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation, and
consequently redirecting propylene oxidation from conventional HClO pathway to a more efficient
•Cl route. This work advances the mechanistic understanding of the mechanism of electrocatalytic
propylene oxidation and offers great opportunities for the sustainable synthesis of commercial
chemicals using waste lithium-ion batteries, seawater, and renewable electricity.

## Introduction

Propylene oxide (PO) is a crucial industrial intermediate, serving as a precursor to a variety of
commercial chemicals including polymers, propylene glycol, polyurethane foams, and propylene
carbonate.1 It ranks as the third most significant propylene derivative with an annual global
production exceeding 10 million tonnes.2 Conventional industrial methods for PO production
include chlorohydrin process, hydrogen peroxide-based process (HPPO) and Halcon process (Fig.
1a-c).3 Nevertheless, these methods face challenges such as high costs, generation of
stoichiometric side products and severe pollution.4 Therefore, there is an urgent demand to develop
a more sustainable PO synthetic route. The electrochemical oxidation of propylene driven by
renewable electricity presents a promising alternative for PO production under ambient
conditions.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 While direct electrooxidation via water-derived active oxygen species offers
a viable route but is severely hindered by propylene’s poor solubility and inevitable overoxidation,
resulting in limited Faradaic efficiency (F.E.) (<70%), low current density (<10 mA cm-2) and
insufficient stability (<12 h), rendering the efficiency of direct electrocatalytic oxidation of
propylene far from satisfactory (Fig. 1d).11, 12, 13, 14

The indirect chlorination-mediated route overcomes these limitations by integrating
electrochemical chloroxidation with propylene oxidation, enabling stable chloropropanol
production which subsequently reacts with the base generated from the cathodic hydrogen
evolution reaction to yield PO (Fig. 1e).2 Notably, besides serving as a redox mediator, chloride
provide the additional advantage of allowing direct use of seawater as the electrolyte. Current
studies identify hypochlorous acid (HClO) as the active species in chlorination-mediated olefin
oxidation, generated through the oxidation of Cl– to Cl
2
, followed by Cl
2
disproportionation with
H
2
O.15 Despite achieving high current density and selectivity, the spontaneous irreversible
decomposition of HClO into non-reactive ClO– still hampers the F.E.16 Furthermore, the oxidized
Cl⁻ were partially reduced back to unreactive HCl during the stoichiometric disproportionation
reaction that formed HClO, resulting in inefficient charge utilization and additional energy
losses.17, 18 In addition, the competitive oxygen evolution reaction (OER) further constrains the
F.E., as the standard electrode potential for chlorine evolution reaction (CER) (1.36 V vs. RHE)
exceeds that of OER (1.23 V vs. RHE).19 Due to the limited utilization of active chlorine species
and the significant OER side reaction, achieving chlorine-mediated electrooxidation of propylene
with high efficiency remains a significant challenge.

Chlorine radicals (•Cl), as a potent oxidant with high oxidation potentials (2.47 V) have been an
appealing option for mediating various oxidation reactions.20, 21, 22, 23, 24 As an electrophilic reagent,
•Cl can react with unsaturated organics such as olefins in addition reactions to form C-Cl bonds
by generating a stabilized secondary carbon-centered radical.25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30 Therefore, the
utilization of •Cl holds great promise for achieving efficient propylene oxidation. During
electrochemical chloroxidation, •Cl is typically produced via the Volmer step.31 Nevertheless, the
marked tendency of •Cl to mutual couple to generate Cl limits its effective utilization. Modulating
2
the adsorption behavior of Cl– on the catalyst surface is expected to reduce the probability of
coupling. For instance, Zhang et al. utilized discontinuous Cl– adsorption sites to inhibit Cl
2
evolution, thereby harnessing •Cl for the electrosynthesis of α,α-dichloroketones.32 Similarly, Liu
et al. enhanced •Cl utilization by increasing the spatial separation between •Cl species, which
mitigated mutual recombination and facilitated the •Cl-mediated epoxide ring-opening process.33
However, due to the lack of direct regulation over the intrinsic adsorption behavior of Cl–, the
utilization efficiency of •Cl remains suboptimal.

Herein, by precisely modulating Cl– adsorption configuration, we realized efficient •Cl-mediated
conversion of propylene to PO on Li-doped Co O , resulting in a production rate of 20.6 mol/m2/h,
3 4
representing 5.2 and 1.4 times higher over pristine Co O and commercial RuIrTi anodes, along
3 4
with a F.E. of 99.0% and long-term stability for over 100 h. Furthermore, a high PO yield of 78.9
mol/m2/h was obtained even under an industrial-level current density of 0.5 A cm-2. Mechanistic
studies revealed that Li doping altered Cl– adsorption configuration on Co O from a linear Co-Cl
3 4

generation and utilization of •Cl species. This enhancement in •Cl availability effectively

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Ming Cheng and co-workers report electrochemical propylene oxide synthesis using Li–Co3O4 catalysts. The authors claim that Li doping reconfigures chloride adsorption on the cobalt oxide surface, thereby promoting a chlorine radical–mediated pathway. They support this with spectroscopic analyses (EPR, FT-IR) and computational studies. The catalytic performance is impressive, and the mechanistic proposal is intriguing. I would recommend publication after the following issues are addressed:
i) A central claim is that propylene oxidation proceeds via chlorine radicals. The in situ EPR study is presented as key evidence, but the Methods section lacks critical details. Please provide a clear description of the spin-trapping protocol (concentration of trapping agents, timing of addition, acquisition parameters). Also, control experiments should be conducted to confirm that spin traps do not interfere with the electrolysis.
ii) The EPR data suggest the involvement of both •Cl and •OH, yet only tert-butanol quenching is reported. Additional radical scavengers or spin trapping (e.g., benzoquinone, BMPO (5-tert-Butoxycarbonyl-5-methyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide), or TEMPO) would provide complementary mechanistic evidence.
iii) The manuscript emphasizes chlorine radicals but also shows stronger •OH signals. The authors attribute this to H2O activation at oxygen vacancies. How do •Cl and •OH interact in the reaction network? Is there any possibility of overoxidation by •OH at higher potentials that could compromise PO selectivity?
iv) A D2O/H2O kinetic isotope effect (KIE) study may help to confirm the hydroxyl involvement in the epoxidation process.
v) Electrochemical analysis requires clarification. Potentials are presented without iR-compensation and referenced to Ag/AgCl, making comparisons with CER/OER a bit ambiguous. Please provide iR-corrected polarization curves, convert potentials to the RHE scale, and quantify solution resistance and membrane contributions by EIS. Reported onset shifts and performance enhancements should be re-evaluated accordingly, to show that the obtained results are intrinsic to Li doping rather than ohmic artifacts.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors successfully incorporated Li into Co3O4 via flash Joule heating treatment, attained a remarkable propylene oxide (PO) Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a production rate of 20.6 mol m-2 h-1 in simulated neutral seawater, along with excellent stability exceeding 100 hours. Mechanistic investigations revealed that HClO was the primary active species in the Co3O4-catalyzed oxidation process, while on Li-Co3O4, the more efficient •Cl pathway becomes dominant. This shift in reaction mechanism is attributed to the Li doping transformed the Cl- adsorption configuration from a linear Co-Cl structure to a more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation. This work not only demonstrates a promising route for utilizing seawater resources in organic synthesis but also offers new mechanistic insights into chlorine-mediated electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. However, there are some shortcomings in the manuscripts.
1. In this paper, the author highlights the advantages of the •Cl pathway over the HClO route. However, radicals are generally known for their inherent lack of selectivity. Why the •Cl-mediated process in this system still achieves high selectivity towards propylene oxide? The author should give more discussion.
2. In Figure 3b, the RuIrTi electrode shows the highest HClO production, yet the Faradaic efficiency for PO is comparable to that of Co3O4. This observation appears inconsistent and needs further explanation.
3. In Figure 4c, the experimental Raman spectrum lacks the peak at 155 cm-1 that is present in the simulated spectrum. The author should give more discussion.
4. In line 275, the formation of HClO on Co3O4 is attributed to the evolution of Cl2. However, HClO could also be generated through the direct oxidation of Cl- (Appl. Catal. B-Environ. Energy 2025, 361, 124644). The authors should provide the corresponding evidence.
5. In the proposed mechanism, the authors suggest that transient and highly reactive •OH attacks transient carbon radical intermediates to form chloropropanol. However, the selectivity and efficiency of coupling between two transient, highly reactive free radicals are theoretically limited (Sci. China Chem. 2025, 68, 3770-3777, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2018, 140, 2438−2441). The authors should reconsider this pathway or supply additional data to validate the role of •OH.
6. Figure 3a shows a significant enhancement in the Cl⁻ reduction peak intensity following the addition and removal of cyclopropane, despite no theoretical change in chloride ion concentration. The authors should provide an explanation and discussion for this discrepancy.
7. All electrode potentials presented in the text and figures should be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale to ensure consistent and standardized reporting.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the author designed a catalyst by doping lithium recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries into Co₃O₄, enabling highly efficient electrocatalytic synthesis of propylene oxide in simulated seawater via enhanced active chlorine generation. This whole work not only offers new insights into the mechanism of propylene epoxidation but also opens a new pathway for environmentally sustainable and low-cost synthesis of industrial chemicals. There are only two minor questions that need to be supplemented:
1. The Li-Co₃O₄ catalyst exhibited good stability during the 100-hour test. Is there any data indicating that Li⁺ does not leach or migrate under strong anodic polarization conditions? Is it necessary to perform post-reaction characterization (such as ICP or XPS) of the catalyst to confirm the retention of Li and the local structural stability?
2. In the catalyst preparation process, flash Joule heating was employed to treat Li-doped Co₃O₄. The article merely mentioned the treatment steps without elaborating on the relevant flash Joule heating parameters (such as heating rate, holding time). The author may supplement as necessary.

### Reviewer 4

This study presents a incorporates lithium into Co₃O₄ via flash Joule heating treatment, achieving efficient chlorine radical-mediated conversion of propylene to propylene oxide (PO), with an excellent PO Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m²/h in simulated neutral seawater, maintaining long-term stability for over 100 hours. This study provides new insights into the mechanism of electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. Overall, this work holds potential for publication in Nature Communications, but several major issues must be addressed to enhance experimental rigor and clarity before I can recommend for its publication.
Major revisions:
1. Through FT-EXAFS analysis, the authors concluded that Li preferentially replaces tetrahedral Co sites (as evidenced by the significant weakening of the Co-Co Td signal) and constructed a corresponding structural model. Did the authors perform theoretical calculations to support this selective replacement tendency? What is the energy difference between Li⁺ entering tetrahedral and octahedral sites? Are there other possible Li occupation sites (such as interstitial sites)?
2. The TOF-SIMS results (Figures 1c-1d) showed a higher concentration of Li in fractured flake regions. Does this imply that the Li doping process is influenced by material morphology or defect density? Could such non-uniform distribution induce compromise the reproducibility of overall catalytic performance?
3. Multiple characterization techniques indicated that Li has entered the lattice and induced changes in electronic structure and local coordination environment, however, no noticeable peak shifts were observed in the XRD patterns (Figure S2). Could the authors explain why no detectable lattice expansion or contraction occurs upon Li doping? Is this due to the low doping level, or could it be attributed to the similar ionic radii of Li⁺ and Co²⁺? Please provide ICP or other quantitative analyses to confirm the actual Li doping content.
4. In the active chlorine (AC) generation (Figure S11) and propylene oxidation tests (Figure 2b), for both Co₃O₄ and RuIrTi catalysts, the lost Faradaic efficiency, could this be attributed to OER or other side reactions? At least, the FE for OER should be measured at one potential to clarify the fate of the missing electrons (FE).
5. During the stability test in Figure 2h, the reaction potential is extremely high (up to 3.6 V vs. Ag/AgCl or may be > 4 V vs. RHE?), which appears inconsistent with the LSV results in Figure 2a. This observation is quite surprising, as both the catalysts and carbon paper substrate remain stable at such a high potential. Have the authors did any characterizations of the catalyst after stability reaction?
6. Theoretical calculations suggest that the OER energy barrier is reduced on Li-Co₃O₄ (Figure 3i). However, during the OER test in Figure 2a, the OER performance of Li-Co₃O₄ shows no improvement compared to Co₃O₄, which seems contradictory. Could the authors discuss this discrepancy?

However, the real electrochemical environment involves a solid–liquid interface. So can these gas-phase-based methods or characterizations accurately reflect the adsorption behavior of the catalyst under actual operating conditions?

Other minor comments:
1. Regarding the O 1s XPS spectra, more detailed assignment of different oxygen species should be provided, rather than simply labeling them with α, β or γ.
2. The manuscript should include more experimental details. The current version lacks sufficient information, making it confusing and difficult to follow. For example, various reaction solutions, including artificial seawater and real seawater are used in experiments in Figure 2. The exact composition of the artificial seawater should be specified, and it should be clarified whether the electrolytes used in Figure 2g–2h are identical to those in Figure 2a.
3. The LSV tests with propylene and NaCl should also be provided, similar to Figure 2a.
4. The assignment of EPR signals for Cl• and OH• radicals should be supported by cited references or spectral simulations in Figure 3d.

## Abstract

Electrocatalytic chlorine-mediated propylene oxidation utilizing seawater represents a
promising route for sustainable propylene oxide (PO) synthesis. Unfortunately, inefficient
utilization of active chlorine species results in compromised yield and Faradaic efficiency (F.E.).
Herein, we achieve efficient chlorine radical-mediated propylene to PO by incorporating Li into
Co O , attaining a PO F.E. approaching 99.0% and a yield of 20.6 mol/m2/h in simulated seawater
3 4
with long-term stability for over 100 h. Furthermore, a PO yield of 78.9 mol/m2/h is obtained even
under an industrial-level current density of 0.5 A cm-2, demonstrating competitive performance
compared with most reported noble metal catalysts. Mechanistic investigations reveal that Li
doping transforms the adsorption configuration of Cl– on Co O from linear Co-Cl structure to
3 4
more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation, and
consequently redirecting propylene oxidation from conventional HClO pathway to a more efficient
•Cl route. This work advances the mechanistic understanding of the mechanism of electrocatalytic
propylene oxidation and offers great opportunities for the sustainable synthesis of commercial
chemicals using waste lithium-ion batteries, seawater, and renewable electricity.

## Introduction

Propylene oxide (PO) is a crucial industrial intermediate, serving as a precursor to a variety of
commercial chemicals including polymers, propylene glycol, polyurethane foams, and propylene
carbonate.1 It ranks as the third most significant propylene derivative with an annual global
production exceeding 10 million tonnes.2 Conventional industrial methods for PO production
include chlorohydrin process, hydrogen peroxide-based process (HPPO) and Halcon process (Fig.
1a-c).3 Nevertheless, these methods face challenges such as high costs, generation of
stoichiometric side products and severe pollution.4 Therefore, there is an urgent demand to develop
a more sustainable PO synthetic route. The electrochemical oxidation of propylene driven by
renewable electricity presents a promising alternative for PO production under ambient
conditions.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 While direct electrooxidation via water-derived active oxygen species offers
a viable route but is severely hindered by propylene’s poor solubility and inevitable overoxidation,
resulting in limited Faradaic efficiency (F.E.) (<70%), low current density (<10 mA cm-2) and
insufficient stability (<12 h), rendering the efficiency of direct electrocatalytic oxidation of
propylene far from satisfactory (Fig. 1d).11, 12, 13, 14

The indirect chlorination-mediated route overcomes these limitations by integrating
electrochemical chloroxidation with propylene oxidation, enabling stable chloropropanol
production which subsequently reacts with the base generated from the cathodic hydrogen
evolution reaction to yield PO (Fig. 1e).2 Notably, besides serving as a redox mediator, chloride
provide the additional advantage of allowing direct use of seawater as the electrolyte. Current
studies identify hypochlorous acid (HClO) as the active species in chlorination-mediated olefin
oxidation, generated through the oxidation of Cl– to Cl
2
, followed by Cl
2
disproportionation with
H
2
O.15 Despite achieving high current density and selectivity, the spontaneous irreversible
decomposition of HClO into non-reactive ClO– still hampers the F.E.16 Furthermore, the oxidized
Cl⁻ were partially reduced back to unreactive HCl during the stoichiometric disproportionation
reaction that formed HClO, resulting in inefficient charge utilization and additional energy
losses.17, 18 In addition, the competitive oxygen evolution reaction (OER) further constrains the
F.E., as the standard electrode potential for chlorine evolution reaction (CER) (1.36 V vs. RHE)
exceeds that of OER (1.23 V vs. RHE).19 Due to the limited utilization of active chlorine species
and the significant OER side reaction, achieving chlorine-mediated electrooxidation of propylene
with high efficiency remains a significant challenge.

Chlorine radicals (•Cl), as a potent oxidant with high oxidation potentials (2.47 V) have been an
appealing option for mediating various oxidation reactions.20, 21, 22, 23, 24 As an electrophilic reagent,
•Cl can react with unsaturated organics such as olefins in addition reactions to form C-Cl bonds
by generating a stabilized secondary carbon-centered radical.25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30 Therefore, the
utilization of •Cl holds great promise for achieving efficient propylene oxidation. During
electrochemical chloroxidation, •Cl is typically produced via the Volmer step.31 Nevertheless, the
marked tendency of •Cl to mutual couple to generate Cl limits its effective utilization. Modulating

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Ming Cheng and co-workers report electrochemical propylene oxide synthesis using Li–Co3O4 catalysts. The authors claim that Li doping reconfigures chloride adsorption on the cobalt oxide surface, thereby promoting a chlorine radical–mediated pathway. They support this with spectroscopic analyses (EPR, FT-IR) and computational studies. The catalytic performance is impressive, and the mechanistic proposal is intriguing. I would recommend publication after the following issues are addressed:
i) A central claim is that propylene oxidation proceeds via chlorine radicals. The in situ EPR study is presented as key evidence, but the Methods section lacks critical details. Please provide a clear description of the spin-trapping protocol (concentration of trapping agents, timing of addition, acquisition parameters). Also, control experiments should be conducted to confirm that spin traps do not interfere with the electrolysis.
ii) The EPR data suggest the involvement of both •Cl and •OH, yet only tert-butanol quenching is reported. Additional radical scavengers or spin trapping (e.g., benzoquinone, BMPO (5-tert-Butoxycarbonyl-5-methyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide), or TEMPO) would provide complementary mechanistic evidence.
iii) The manuscript emphasizes chlorine radicals but also shows stronger •OH signals. The authors attribute this to H2O activation at oxygen vacancies. How do •Cl and •OH interact in the reaction network? Is there any possibility of overoxidation by •OH at higher potentials that could compromise PO selectivity?
iv) A D2O/H2O kinetic isotope effect (KIE) study may help to confirm the hydroxyl involvement in the epoxidation process.
v) Electrochemical analysis requires clarification. Potentials are presented without iR-compensation and referenced to Ag/AgCl, making comparisons with CER/OER a bit ambiguous. Please provide iR-corrected polarization curves, convert potentials to the RHE scale, and quantify solution resistance and membrane contributions by EIS. Reported onset shifts and performance enhancements should be re-evaluated accordingly, to show that the obtained results are intrinsic to Li doping rather than ohmic artifacts.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors successfully incorporated Li into Co3O4 via flash Joule heating treatment, attained a remarkable propylene oxide (PO) Faradaic efficiency approaching 99.0% and a production rate of 20.6 mol m-2 h-1 in simulated neutral seawater, along with excellent stability exceeding 100 hours. Mechanistic investigations revealed that HClO was the primary active species in the Co3O4-catalyzed oxidation process, while on Li-Co3O4, the more efficient •Cl pathway becomes dominant. This shift in reaction mechanism is attributed to the Li doping transformed the Cl- adsorption configuration from a linear Co-Cl structure to a more favorable triangular Li-Cl-O configuration, thereby enhancing •Cl generation. This work not only demonstrates a promising route for utilizing seawater resources in organic synthesis but also offers new mechanistic insights into chlorine-mediated electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. However, there are some shortcomings in the manuscripts.
1. In this paper, the author highlights the advantages of the •Cl pathway over the HClO route. However, radicals are generally known for their inherent lack of selectivity. Why the •Cl-mediated process in this system still achieves high selectivity towards propylene oxide? The author should give more discussion.
2. In Figure 3b, the RuIrTi electrode shows the highest HClO production, yet the Faradaic efficiency for PO is comparable to that of Co3O4. This observation appears inconsistent and needs further explanation.
3. In Figure 4c, the experimental Raman spectrum lacks the peak at 155 cm-1 that is present in the simulated spectrum. The author should give more discussion.
4. In line 275, the formation of HClO on Co3O4 is attributed to the evolution of Cl2. However, HClO could also be generated through the direct oxidation of Cl- (Appl. Catal. B-Environ. Energy 2025, 361, 124644). The authors should provide the corresponding evidence.
5. In the proposed mechanism, the authors suggest that transient and highly reactive •OH attacks transient carbon radical intermediates to form chloropropanol. However, the selectivity and efficiency of coupling between two transient, highly reactive free radicals are theoretically limited (Sci. China Chem. 2025, 68, 3770-3777, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2018, 140, 2438−2441). The authors should reconsider this pathway or supply additional data to validate the role of •OH.
6. Figure 3a shows a significant enhancement in the Cl⁻ reduction peak intensity following the addition and removal of cyclopropane, despite no theoretical change in chloride ion concentration. The authors should provide an explanation and discussion for this discrepancy.
7. All electrode potentials presented in the text and figures should be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale to ensure consistent and standardized reporting.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the author designed a catalyst by doping lithium recovered from spent lithium-ion batteries into Co₃O₄, enabling highly efficient electrocatalytic synthesis of propylene oxide in simulated seawater via enhanced active chlorine generation. This whole work not only offers new insights into the mechanism of propylene epoxidation but also opens a new pathway for environmentally sustainable and low-cost synthesis of industrial chemicals. There are only two minor questions that need to be supplemented:
1. The Li-Co₃O₄ catalyst exhibited good stability during the 100-hour test. Is there any data indicating that Li⁺ does not leach or migrate under strong anodic polarization conditions? Is it necessary to perform post-reaction characterization (such as ICP or XPS) of the catalyst to confirm the retention of Li and the local structural stability?
2. In the catalyst preparation process, flash Joule heating was employed to treat Li-doped Co₃O₄. The article merely mentioned the treatment steps without elaborating on the relevant flash Joule heating parameters (such as heating rate, holding time). The author may supplement as necessary.

### Reviewer 4

This study provides new insights into the mechanism of electrocatalytic propylene oxidation. Overall, this work holds potential for publication in Nature Communications, but several major issues must be addressed to enhance experimental rigor and clarity before I can recommend for its publication.
Major revisions:
1. Through FT-EXAFS analysis, the authors concluded that Li preferentially replaces tetrahedral Co sites (as evidenced by the significant weakening of the Co-Co Td signal) and constructed a corresponding structural model. Did the authors perform theoretical calculations to support this selective replacement tendency? What is the energy difference between Li⁺ entering tetrahedral and octahedral sites? Are there other possible Li occupation sites (such as interstitial sites)?

Multiple characterization techniques indicated that Li has entered the lattice and induced changes in electronic structure and local coordination environment, however, no noticeable peak shifts were observed in the XRD patterns (Figure S2).
